articles.title: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon
articles.summary: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand? I must admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena.
body: John Cena is a company man. The word “loyalty” comes up often, and about everything from his friends back home to the wrestling to the US itself. Admirable, no doubt. But Cena’s loyalty has drawn him into some uncomfortable positions, and for 20 minutes our good-natured chat about reliability, discipline and what it means to owe everything to something bigger than yourself has set us on a collision course with one of the most disgraced figures in modern entertainment.

Cena was born in West Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1977, one of five boys in a household that watched every dollar. His grandma and grandpa lived in an adjoining house. “There was a lot of ‘How are we going to pay the bills, how are we going to keep the lights on?’” Cena says. He worshipped the movie action men of the era – Schwarzenegger, Stallone, Willis – but he also loved hip-hop, which in suburban Massachusetts made him a target for bullies. Bodybuilding was the answer, and it doubles as an origin story – the boy bullied for dressing like a white rapper, growing up to become an icon for the next generation of suburban youth.

articles.title: The hidden daytime dance revolution - and the man who captured it on camera
articles.summary: Tim Smith's shots of the early 'daytimers' bhangra scene in Bradford feature in a Tate exhibition.
body: For decades, photographer Tim Smith's images of Bradford's British Asian "daytimers" dance scene remained largely unseen. Now, some of those shots are taking their place in a major Tate exhibition examining the creativity and rebellion that transformed 1990s Britain.
On a bright afternoon in Bradford, shoppers moved through the city centre carrying bags, going about their day.
Behind a nearby doorway, another side of Bradford was pulsing to a very different rhythm.
Tim Smith remembers stepping out of a small nightclub beneath the Alhambra theatre after spending hours photographing a "daytimers" disco.

articles.title: The Feeling album recorded in a Sussex shed
articles.summary: The Feeling's debut album turns 20 as the band prepare for Eastbourne and Margate shows.
body: The Feeling's triple-platinum debut album was recorded in a shed in Horsham, according to frontman Dan Gillespie Sells.
Speaking to BBC Radio Sussex as the record marks its 20th anniversary, Gillespie Sells said it came from "a very different world" when music fans bought CDs and "nobody had an iPhone".
The singer said much of Twelve Stops and Home was made at the Sussex home of brothers and bandmates Kevin and Ciaran Jeremiah.
The Feeling will perform the album in full when a 20th anniversary tour visits Eastbourne and Margate in November.

articles.title: The Kent village that helped shape Audrey Hepburn
articles.summary: Audrey Hepburn spent three years in Elham before the outbreak of World War Two.
body: Long before she became one of Hollywood's most celebrated stars, Audrey Hepburn was learning music and dance at a small village school in the Kent countryside.

The future Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady actress spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, where local historians say her love of performing was encouraged during three formative years before the outbreak of World War Two.
Today, a blue plaque on a cottage near the King's Arms pub marks the place where Hepburn lived between 1936 and 1939.
"It really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," said Brian Badham, of Elham Historical Society.

articles.title: ‘A Statement’ Review: Just What We Need Right Now — Another Movie About Climate Change! But Tom McCarthy’s Historically Based Talkfest Reveals How Much We Knew in 1980
articles.summary: On paper, "A Statement" sounds like an interesting movie, but it’s at once talky and flat, grabby and meandering, impassioned and neutral. It wants to be a "firebrand" docudrama, yet I can’t imagine who the audience is going to be for it. My heartless prediction: next to no one.
body: The film presents, exactly as it happened, a conference of officials assigned to advise Congress on the global-warming crisis. But their talk doesn't quite become action.

McCarthy and his co-screenwriters, Thomas Bidegain and Noé Debré, decided not to “dramatize” the conference. Instead, they dug the dialogue right out of the actual transcripts, presenting the conversations verbatim, which is on some level a daring choice. And McCarthy is certainly a skilled enough filmmaker to get the effect he was going for. In “A Statement,” he catches the sound and rhythm, the verbal wheel-spinning, the fuddy-duddy quibbling essence of that thing known as a strategic planning meeting.

articles.title: 5 Genre-Defining Sci-Fi Movies That Barely Impacted The Box Office
articles.summary: The 5 sci-fi movies on this list all underperformed or downright flopped at the box office, and yet their influence on the genre has been massive.
body: Sometimes hits are forgotten, and sometimes bombs become hits. Some of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time bombed at the box office.

And, just as often, the opposite will occur. A box office bomb can be hastily swept out of theaters, ignored by audiences, and sometimes even lambasted by critics. But then, years later, repertory screenings and home video consumption will invite a grand relitigation of said movies, and the critical tide will turn. Additionally, some important young filmmakers will be influenced by those bombs, make movies in their likeness, and the one-time box office failure will suddenly be culturally important. It's like what Brian Eno said about the Velvet Underground. "The first Velvet Underground album only sold 10,000 copies, but everyone who bought it formed a band."
The following five movies all notoriously tanked at the box office, but are now considered sci-fi standards among the genre's fans.
